doc.title: Josephine Davies interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 14, 2025

title: Studio takes, live albums and editing technology
summary: She prefers authentic, lively takes to polished ones, favours live playing, and is wary of editing out imperfections.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: And do you have a sense of – you do a take and everybody in the trio says, “That’s it. We don’t need to do that one again.”?

Yeah. That’s the best case scenario. And I suppose because for me the studio situation is always a challenge because I get so much out of the live playing situation and I really feed off the audience and I love the sense of connection with the bands and the audience and the space and the venue and that way of well this is only happening in this moment, that’s it. You’re never going to hear it again. And actually two of my albums are live albums and they are, I think, arguably the better albums. Who knows? There are good things and bad things because you can’t polish it after it’s happened. So in a studio situation yeah, I’d say that the best case scenario is when you feel like you’ve done a take, that was it. We’ve got nothing more to say, you don’t need to say anything more, it was tight enough, although that’s not my main requirement. The main requirement to me is that everyone says something authentic and there’s something happening and it’s lively and it’s interesting. And then the bits that don’t quite sound as polished as they could be, for me I can let go of that rather than have a very perfect take that’s perhaps not that interesting. Because there’s so much music in the world. You know there’s so much of deep interest that what I’m looking for, what matters so much to me is something different, something alive, something where you can really hear the personality of the musicians. And then to me it doesn’t matter if there’s a bit that’s, you know, the hit between the bass and the drums doesn’t quite happen at the same time while someone plays a fluffed note. And those things are less important to me.
I’m going to guess that perhaps you do not take advantage of the technology that enables us now to get rid of a stray note. Or, “Oh the bass hit this just before the bass drum, let’s move the note.”

I would say that’s a very fair comment. Yes. I don’t necessarily take advantage of all the technology. In some ways maybe I could do more of that but in other ways I think whatever happens on the day happens on the day and that’s what people get. I always think that we as musicians are so overcritical of what happens, our own playing primarily, and we can get really caught up in knots that that could have been better. And the technology allows us to make changes that we wouldn’t otherwise be able to. And there’s something about that, that I can never make a definitive statement of what’s right and wrong with the different – and different genres of music will require different technological input. And, but I guess there’s always a question mark for me around how much are we going to edit a jazz performance? Is that what John Coltrane would have done?
